narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 56.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the second decile, noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. This signal of relative academic standing in law school carried the most weight.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and worked in your favor. At 39, you scored above the average of 37.2 seen in accepted applicants, which helped pull the prediction back toward passing. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.10 was the third most influential feature. It sat slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore nudged the outcome modestly toward failure.

Taken together, the lower third-year class rank outweighed the positive effect of your LSAT and the small negative effect of your GPA, resulting in an overall prediction of likely bar exam failure.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on improving your class rank in the remaining law school years, seek targeted bar-prep support early, and consider reapplying once you have stronger upper-year performance. Many students successfully improve their trajectory after an initial setback.
